barCharacter: Scott Howl (the loud, sincere golden-retriever jock who wants to help and to be told he did well; his comic job is the closest to Brock's)

bar: Cool, okay! I understood… a couple of those words, and I have no further questions. Let's do whatever you just suggested!
Half of my friends are balls, actually! There's Ollie the volleyball, Fergus the golf ball, Troy the basketball - he's the best, he REALLY gets his head in the game…

GASP! That's crazy! I thought they were solved by smart people, but this makes way more sense!
Yay, thank you! You're pretty cool for a god of torture!
Cool! Can we pretty-please borrow your cage?

Don't worry, you'll do fine! But I should warn you that when I'm a wolf I can't really control my base desires. Wolf-Scott isn't as smart as Me-Scott!
GRRRR, WHO AM I? AM I HANDSOME? ... Oh yeah, I'm Scott Howl, and I'm super handsome!
headToHead.voiceJudgement: Cover the names and all twelve of ours are Brock's. The two-beat user report (a named user, a wrong detail, an escalation delivered as good news, then a flat verdict) is now a sentence shape and not only a topic, and no one else in the cast has it. Scott is just as recognisable, but his recognisability comes from range. He does a breathless run-on ('Half of my friends are balls, actually! There's Ollie...'), a one-breath plea ('Cool! Can we pretty-please borrow your cage?'), a self-correction that makes it worse, and a GRRRR. Brock has one rhythm. Nearly every line is four to six full-stopped fragments ending on a flat verdict, and twelve in a row sound like one line read twelve times. Equal on recognisability, the bar on range: a tie.
headToHead.constructionJudgement: Per line, ours is now tighter than Scott's. The turn lands on the last two to four words ('Stretched.', 'Still going down.', 'He books it weekly.', 'It always finishes!', 'One.'), nothing explains itself, and the round-2 note was actually done: users now get a second beat (Walt still going down, the grandson booking it, Kevin moving in, the fridge going upstairs). Several of Scott's lines are flat or lean on the scene around them ('If there are two wolves there, maybe it won't be so weird!', 'It just kinda looks like paper.'). Two weaknesses keep this from being a clean win. Too many escalations only go up in number (Pam banned from three stores, now five; Biscuit at three hundred and one; Ma'am, hourly, then half-hourly) when they should change in kind, the way a beachball falls in love with a thumbtack. And the name-repeat button ('Kevin. Kevin lives with me now.', 'Gary's had worse days. Gary's had all of them.', 'Somebody tell Denise. Somebody tell Denise who I am.') is turning into a tic. Even so, on these twelve, ours.
headToHead.quotableJudgement: 'My intentions are cardiovascular' and 'still going down' are clip buttons, and 'Crumb, I'll pop up first. On three. One.' is a perfect jab. Scott has the bit people retell: the ball friends, and Barry the Beachball's unhealthy relationship with a thumbtack. It is an invented world told as gossip and it survives being summarised. Brock's user world could do that, but each user lives in one line and the lines repeat a shape, so a viewer remembers 'the dog with the users' and not a particular bit. Barry is the line a viewer would quote to a friend tomorrow. The bar wins narrowly, and in doubt the bar wins.

biggestGap: Every line is the same rhythm: four to six full-stopped fragments ending on a flat verdict ('Kevin lives with me now.', 'Marjorie swims now!'). Twelve in a row read like one line read twelve times, while Scott swings between a breathless run-on, a one-breath plea and a GRRRR. In the next pass, rewrite about a third of the bank, starting with the ten race lines and the seven 'X now' buttons, as a single breathless run-on (one user's story chained with 'and', 'but', 'actually', escalating in kind, not in number) or as a one-breath plea to the star, and keep the full-stop staccato only for the lines where the button needs the silence.

notes: I read the bar file (refs/writing/monster-prom-lines.md) in full, plus charm-notes.md, CAST.md, the persona, the types.ts comments and my round-2 verdict for comparison. The bank holds 112 lines and 39 are flagged above: 34.8%, against 37.5% in round 2 and 48.2% in round 1. A line is flagged if any one test catches it. Every line passes the word limits; a script checked each one against 12 for openers, 10 for jabs and 20 for the rest. Round 3 fixed the round-2 problems that needed fixing. The Frost lines are rewritten for Crumb. The reversal ('I don't X. I'm X-ing.') and 'That's a [GYM WORD]' templates are mostly gone. 'Proud' appears once and lands on Walt, which is exactly right. Users now get a second beat. Construction pulls ahead of the bar line for line, and it is the best Brock has been. What replaced the old templates is a new set: the race (10 lines), the 'X now' button (7) and the name-repeat button (9+), all inside one unvaried cadence. Lines worth protecting beyond the top five: 'They laughed! Texting Denise. Denise says 'who is this.' She'll come around.', 'Going home. Nobody there to cheer for. I'll cheer the microwave. It always finishes!', 'Noted. Going to tell Gary. Gary's had worse days. Gary's had all of them.', 'The airport. People run for their gates. We cheer them on. Strangers LOVE it.', 'Vex finished my sentence. Wrong. I was saying LUNGES.', 'Tilly, sorry number nine! Everybody up! One more, Tilly!', 'Good game. Good game. Line up, everybody, handshakes. Why is nobody lining up.', 'Their pulse went up twice tonight. Once for me. Once for a moth. I'm tied with a moth.' Quick wins that need no talent: merge the two Nav lines and the two Hector lines into one each; cut one of the two 'good job, Brock' lines; take the chart away from Brock in the Dash roast; drop 'Great work, Tilly.' The same caveat as round 2 holds: Scott's lines live inside scenes a narrator sets up, while Brock's are drawn at random and must stand alone in 20 words. That helps explain why construction now goes to ours, but the bar still wins on range of voice and on the retold bit.
